title_en: Faith in Revelation and in the Angels
body_ar:
من أركان الإيمان الإيمان بالكتب والإيمان بالملائكة والإيمان بالرسل، فلا يصح إيمان مؤمن إلا بها، لكن الواجب هو الإيمان تفصيلاً بما ورد تفصيله في القرآن والسنة، وما لم يرد تفصيله فإننا نؤمن به إجمالاً.
الإيمان بالوحي:
قال الشيخ حفظه الله: [والوحي حق ليس قولاً يختلق والكتب حق والملائكة حق] ذكر أن مما يجب الإيمان به الوحي. ......
تعريف الوحي:
والوحي في اللغة يطلق على السرعة وعلى الإلهام وعلى الكتابة، فله ثلاثة معان، يقال: وحى وأوحى بمعنى: كتب، وبمعنى: أسرع، وبمعنى: أذهب، ومثلها وخى -بالخاء- وكذلك توخى، ترد أيضاً بهذا المعنى. ومنه قول الشاعر: فلما رأى أن النجاة تعذرت رأى أن ذا الكربين لا يتعذر توخى بها مجرى سهيل ودونه من الشام أجبال تطول وتقصر وورود الوحي بمعنى الإلهام كثير في القرآن، كقول الله تعالى: وَأَوْحَى رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ[النحل:68]...
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* Among the pillars of faith are faith in the books, faith in the angels and faith in the messengers, and no believer's faith is valid without them. What is obligatory (wājib), however, is faith in detail in what has been set out in detail in the Qur'an and the sunnah; what has not been set out in detail, we believe in in summary form.

## Faith in revelation

The Sheikh, may God preserve him, said: *[And revelation is true, not speech that is fabricated; and the books are true, and the angels are true.]* He mentioned that revelation is among the things faith in which is obligatory. ......

## The definition of revelation

In the language, "waḥy" is applied to speed, to inspiration and to writing — so it has three senses. One says "waḥā" and "awḥā" in the sense of "he wrote", in the sense of "he hastened", and in the sense of "he directed". Like it is "wakhā", with khāʾ, and likewise "tawakhkhā", which also occurs in this sense. From it are the words of the poet:

*When he saw that escape had become impossible, he saw that the one burdened with two distresses is not beyond reach; he steered her toward the course of Canopus, though short of it, on the Syrian side, are mountains that rise high and fall low.*

The occurrence of "waḥy" in the sense of inspiration is frequent in the Qur'an, as in the words of God, exalted is He: {And your Lord inspired the bee: take for yourself dwellings in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they build} (Sūrat al-Naḥl 16:68) …

flags.context: the record breaks off and the full text sits behind a download
options: render with an excerpt banner and link the .doc
render as a complete text
flags.note: Excerpt only, style guide section 9. It breaks off on an ellipsis in the middle of the lexical treatment of the word 'waḥy', before revelation in its technical sense is defined and before the angels — half of the title — are reached at all. The complete text sits behind /medias/doc/L-28.doc. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends and completes nothing. Must not be rendered as a whole lesson.

flags.arabic: الفقرة الافتتاحية مقابل ما بعد العنوان الفرعي
flags.context: the synopsis paragraph against the transcribed opening of the lesson
options: mark the synopsis as the site's own and the remainder as the Sheikh's words
present the whole record as the Sheikh's words
flags.note: The record has two authors. The first paragraph is a synopsis written by the site — it speaks about the lesson and its subject in the third person and does not begin with the opening formula. Everything from the section heading onward is transcribed speech in the Sheikh's own voice. The site must not present the synopsis as his words.

flags.context: the formula introducing each quoted line of the versified creed being commented on
options: keep 'the Sheikh' unresolved and record the ambiguity
read it as the author of the versified text, distinct from the lecturer
read it as Sheikh al-Dedew quoting his own verse
flags.note: The referent of 'الشيخ' cannot be settled from the served text, and getting it wrong would misattribute a creedal formulation. These lessons are a commentary on a versified creed (nazm): the transcriber introduces each base-text line with 'the Sheikh, may God preserve him, said', then the commentary follows. 'حفظه الله' is used of the living, which fits Sheikh al-Dedew himself — in which case he is both the author of the verse and its commentator — but the formula is also the ordinary way a transcriber marks the author of a base text. The English leaves 'the Sheikh' unresolved exactly as the Arabic does. The Sheikh's office can settle it in one answer, and it should be settled before publication, because the bracketed verse and the prose around it would then carry different attributions.

flags.arabic: ذكر أن مما يجب الإيمان به الوحي. ......
flags.context: the six dots standing where the commentary on the first verse should be
options: reproduce the source's own ellipsis and supply nothing
treat the gap as a transcription loss and note it
close the gap silently
flags.note: A second break inside the record, distinct from the one at the end. The commentary on the first quoted line is reduced to a single sentence followed by six dots, and the text then resumes under a fresh heading. Whatever was said about faith in the books and in the angels — two of the three things the quoted verse affirms and half of the record's title — is missing here and not merely cut off at the end. The dots are the source's own and are reproduced; nothing has been supplied.

flags.context: the third of three glosses on the verb وحى / أوحى
options: in the sense of 'he directed'
in the sense of 'he made to go'
read a transcription error for أومأ, 'he signalled'
flags.note: The passage does not cohere as served and the reviewer should see why. Three lexical senses are announced — speed, inspiration and writing — and three glosses are then given: 'he wrote', 'he hastened' and 'أذهب'. The third gloss matches none of the three announced senses, and inspiration, which is announced, is left without a gloss. The line of verse that follows illustrates 'توخى' in the sense of aiming or steering toward something, which supports reading 'أذهب' as directing or making something go, and that is what the English gives. It may equally be a transcription error. Nothing has been corrected; style guide section 11.

flags.arabic: رأى أن ذا الكربين لا يتعذر
flags.context: the first hemistich-pair of the cited verse
options: he saw that the one burdened with two distresses is not beyond reach
he saw that the man of the two afflictions is not impossible to find
he saw that what has two hardships is not out of reach
flags.note: 'ذو الكربين' is not identified in the served text and the couplet is cited without its author. Read against the second line — steering a mount by Canopus across mountainous country — the sense is that one course remains open when escape by any other has closed, but the referent of the epithet is genuinely unclear and the English is provisional. Flagged rather than resolved.

flags.arabic: فلا يصح إيمان مؤمن إلا بها
options: no believer's faith is valid without them
no believer's faith is sound without them
no one's faith counts as faith without them
flags.note: 'صحيح' of an act is 'valid', of a hadith 'sound'; the glossary is explicit that context decides, and the subject here is a person's faith, not a report. 'Valid' also keeps the statement about the standing of the act and not about its moral quality.

options: what is obligatory (wājib) is faith in detail
what is required is belief in the particulars
flags.note: A ruling, and it is the site's word rather than the Sheikh's — the transcribed portion never reaches the detailed/summary distinction. Rendered 'obligatory' per the fixed mapping. The distinction it states (الإيمان تفصيلاً / إجمالاً) is treated at length in record 714 of this same run, where the Sheikh does speak in his own voice; a reader should be sent there rather than take the synopsis for his position.

translator_notes: One of a run of fifteen records, IDs 707-721, in the written-creed section, all uploaded on 9 and 10 May 2011 within a few hours of one another, all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/L-* series, numbered L-26 to L-39 in the same order as the IDs. The uniform timestamps are a bulk upload and say nothing about when the lesson was delivered.

The record contains two distinct voices and the English keeps them apart. The opening paragraph is a synopsis written by the site, about the lesson and in the third person; everything from the section heading onward is the Sheikh's own words as transcribed. Nothing in the synopsis may be quoted as his.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.
Qur'anic renderings here are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic.

This record is doubly broken: once in the middle, where the commentary on the first verse is replaced by six dots, and once at the end. Of the two subjects in its title, revelation is treated only lexically and the angels are never reached.
The line of verse is rendered as prose in italics per style guide section 4; no rhymed English has been attempted and the Arabic is kept in body_ar for the bilingual pane.

'سهيل' is the star Canopus, used as a navigational marker in classical Arabic verse; the English names the star rather than transliterating, since the point of the citation is the act of steering by it.
